content: The document discusses the cost-effectiveness and clinical implications of implementing an indeterminate range for early infant diagnosis of HIV, particularly in settings with limited resources. 1. HIV in Infants and Children: HIV remains a significant cause of illness and death among infants and children, especially in lowand middle-income countries. Historically, mother-to-child transmission of HIV was difficult to control in these regions. However, the advent of highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART) and its increased availability and affordability have led to significant progress in preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. As a result, transmission rates have steadily declined and are expected to continue decreasing with the global scale-up of PMTCT programs. 2. Challenges with HIV Diagnosis in Infants: Despite the success of PMTCT programs, unintended complications have emerged. The positive predictive value (PPV) of HIV diagnostic tests is closely tied to the prevalence of HIV among exposed infants. As transmission rates decrease, the PPV of diagnostic tests also declines, increasing the likelihood of false-positive results. To address this, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all positive HIV test results be confirmed with a second test. However, in many settings, such as sub-Saharan Africa, only 10-15% of initial positive tests undergo confirmatory testing. Consequently, some HIV-uninfected infants may be started on lifelong ART without confirmatory test results. 3. Minimizing False-Positive Diagnoses: To reduce the number of false-positive diagnoses and the associated unnecessary ART regimens, it is possible to identify test results that are more likely to be false positives. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) detect the amplification of DNA during multiple cycles of synthesis. A positive result is reported when the DNA level surpasses a control threshold during a specific cycle, known as the cycle threshold (Ct). In samples with HIV DNA, the Ct value is inversely correlated with the amount of DNA present (i.e., a high Ct value corresponds to a low viral load). False-positive results, often due to contamination or technical errors, are typically associated with high Ct values. Therefore, Ct values can provide useful information for distinguishing between true-positive and false-positive results when confirmatory testing is unavailable. 4. Indeterminate Range for Ct Values: The analysis explores the utility, clinical trade-offs, and cost savings of adopting an indeterminate range of Ct values for initial HIV diagnostic tests. This approach involves categorizing test results with high Ct values as indeterminate, rather than positive, and withholding presumptive ART until confirmatory testing is performed. The study demonstrates that this strategy can significantly reduce the number of unnecessary ART regimens prescribed and may become increasingly favorable as PMTCT programs expand. Additionally, prioritizing infants with indeterminate results for confirmatory testing could further enhance the cost-effectiveness of this approach. 5. Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms: Two diagnostic and treatment algorithms were compared in the study: Standard of Care (SoC): Infants with any non-negative test result (positive or indeterminate) are immediately started on presumptive ART. A proportion of these infants do not undergo confirmatory testing and remain on lifelong ART. For those who do undergo confirmatory testing, results are typically available six months later. A negative confirmatory result leads to the suspension of ART, while a non-negative result confirms the need for lifelong ART. Indeterminate Range Algorithm: Infants with low Ct values (high viral load) are treated the same as in the SoC algorithm. However, infants with indeterminate results (high Ct values) do not receive presumptive ART and are only started on lifelong ART if a confirmatory test confirms a non-negative result. Infants with indeterminate results who do not undergo confirmatory testing do not receive ART. This approach represents the key difference from the SoC algorithm. 6. Clinical and Economic Outcomes: The study modeled the outcomes of a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 HIV-exposed infants in sub-Saharan Africa. The analysis included costs associated with testing, presumptive ART care, and lifelong ART. Outcomes of interest included the number of HIV-uninfected individuals unnecessarily started on ART (false positives), the number of HIV-related deaths, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) measured as the cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. The findings suggest that the indeterminate range algorithm can reduce unnecessary ART regimens and associated costs while maintaining acceptable clinical outcomes. 7. Sensitivity Analyses: Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the impact of various factors, such as HIV prevalence and the probability of repeat testing, on model outcomes. A variation of the indeterminate range algorithm was also explored, prioritizing infants with indeterminate results for repeat testing while excluding infants with positive results from repeat testing. This approach further improved the cost-effectiveness of the indeterminate range algorithm. 8. Conclusion: The adoption of an indeterminate range for Ct values in early infant HIV diagnosis is likely to be justified by substantial reductions in unnecessary ART regimens and associated costs. This approach becomes increasingly favorable as PMTCT programs expand globally. Additionally, prioritizing infants with indeterminate results for confirmatory testing can further enhance the clinical and economic benefits of this strategy.
